name: View identity
first: How SwiftUI tells whether a view in a new description is the same view as before, which keeps its state, or a new view, whose state starts again.

dependsOn.why: Identity decides whether a view keeps its state or starts it again.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The property `taps` is state of `Counter`, as it is on the page of State.

dependsOn.why: A view that keeps its identity runs its body again only when a value that the body read changes.
dependsOn.whyInExample: When line 23 gives the renderer a new `Screen`, nothing that the `body` of `Counter` read has changed, as `visits` changed nothing on the page of View update.

what.is: A view's identity is how SwiftUI tells whether a view in a new description is the same view as before. The same view keeps its state, and a new view starts its state again. SwiftUI uses the view's place in its parent's `body`, and the value of its `id` modifier when it has one.
what.afterExample: Lines 23 and 26 give the renderer a new `Screen`. With the same id, `Counter` is the same view, and `taps` stays 1. With a new id, `Counter` is a new view, so `taps` starts again at 0.
what.problem: SwiftUI makes a new description of the screen each time a `body` runs, and each description is made of new values. SwiftUI must match each view in it with a view it already has, to keep that view's state, or else make a new view.
what.how: Apple's documentation says that when the value given to a view's `id` changes, the view's identity, and with it its state, is reset. A view with no `id` is matched by its place: a view of the same type at the same place in its parent's `body` is the same view.

when.text: Use `id` to start a view again on purpose, such as an editor when the user picks a different trip.
Don't give `id` a value that changes each time the `body` runs, such as a new random number. Every update would then make a new view, and its state would be lost each time.

parts.name: The place of `Counter()`, line 15
parts.text: The `body` of `Screen` has one view, `Counter()`, at its first place. In each new `Screen`, a `Counter` is at the same place, so by its place it is the same view.

parts.name: The id, line 15
parts.text: The modifier `id` gives `Counter` the value of `version` as its id. SwiftUI compares it as well as the place: while it stays 1, the view is the same view, and when it becomes 2, the view is a new view.

steps.text: Line 19 makes a `Screen` with version 1, and line 20 makes a renderer. Line 21 asks for the image, so SwiftUI makes a `Counter` with id 1, whose `taps` is 0.
The `body` of `Counter` runs, and line 6 prints {{taps is 0}}.
The `Text` appears, and line 8 adds 1 to `taps`, so the `body` runs again, and line 6 prints {{taps is 1}}.

Line 23 gives the renderer a new `Screen`, with version 1 again, and line 24 draws it. The `Counter` is at the same place with the same id, so it is the same view, and `taps` is still 1. Nothing that its `body` read changed, so the `body` does not run.

Line 26 gives the renderer a `Screen` with version 2, and line 27 draws it. The id changed, so SwiftUI removes the old `Counter` and makes a new one, whose `taps` starts at 0. Line 6 prints {{taps is 0}}.
The new `Text` appears, line 8 adds 1 to `taps`, and line 6 prints {{taps is 1}}.

end.text: The same place and the same id kept the view and its state. A new id made a new view, whose state started again.
